messages.subject: help with marginal WAIC w/ grouping
messages.subject_clean: help with marginal WAIC w/ grouping
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nimble Community,

I am struggling with calculating WAIC for a integrated model. The model has a multi-state component, where I am using marginal likelihood to avoid estimating the true latent states (z). The likelihood component for this portion is

 for(i in 1:marked){
    y[i,f[i]:l[i]] ~ dHMM(probInit = TLM[spz[i],fs[i],1:15],
                          probObs = OPM[R[i],1:15,1:17],
                          probTrans = TPM[spz[i],f[i]:(l[i]-1),1:15,1:15],
                          len=length(f[i]:l[i]))

  }

where y is the observed state of fish i. I believe since I am using marginal likelihood, and since dHMM returns onee likelihood value for each fish's capture history I should use marginal WAIC for node y, and groups y[i,f[i]:l[i]]. Is this correct? My waic control arguments are

for(i in 1:constants$marked){groups[i]<-paste0('y[',i,',',constants$f[i],':',constants$l[i],']')}
list(dataGroups=groups,MarginalizeNodes='y').

The second portion of the model is a multinomial glm. The likelihood is as follows

  for(i in 1:lrow){
    marr[i,1:175]~dmulti(pi[i,1:175],n[i])
  }

should I group nodes marr[i,1:175] as well since one likelihood value is calculated for each row in marr?

Thanks for all the help. I am very new to WAIC.

Best,
Max

On Sunday, February 4, 2024 at 2:04:33 PM UTC-6 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> Heather and others following this thread,
>
> Version 1.1.0, just released last week, should substantially smooth out the process of using nimbleHMC for models with discrete distributions. In particular, automatic differentiation (AD) can be used in a wider range of  models, including models with stochastic indexing, discrete latent states, and CAR distributions. Support for AD for these models means that HMC sampling and Laplace approximation can be used, although of course HMC samplers can only be assigned to nodes following continuous distributions. In addition, version 1.1.0 now allows distributions and functions (whether user-defined or built-in) that lack AD support (such as dinterval, dconstraint, and truncated distributions) to be used and compiled in AD-enabled models. The added flexibility increases the range of models in which one can use AD methods (HMC or Laplace) on some parts of a model and other samplers or methods on other parts.
>
> We've updated this section <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-AD.html#what-operations-are-and-arent-supported-for-ad> of the manual to try to be clear about what is and is not supported by AD and implications for derivative-based methods such as HMC.
>
> -chris
>
>
>

> >
> > The issue is discrete distributions for latent states, like dcat and dconstraint, for which there is no way around that the code won't compile (and/or won't give correct results) even if you don't want to use derivatives involving those nodes. I believe that is a problem whether the distribution "d" function is used directly in a model or in a user-defined function or distribution.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Max,
I actually don't see any errors there. Those are warnings that turn out to be harmless.  It is voluminous and alarming at first, but there's not much we can do about it. They come from the Eigen linear algebra package that we use. Eigen actually has a file in its source code called "DisableStupidWarnings.h" that uses C++ #pragma (pre-processor) statements do disable these warnings, but CRAN policy disallows disabling of C++ warnings in this way and scans code to catch violations of its policy, so we have to let the warning fly at you (if you have showCompilerOutput=TRUE). In general it is difficult to manage C++ compiler warnings because users may be running many variants of C++ compilers and configurations. That's why by default the C++ compiler output is not shown by compileNimble. If you are getting output that shows errors (typically with the word "error"), please send a reproducible example. Thanks and HTH.
Perry

Hi Perry,

Thanks for the quick response. I am running into an issue when compiling, Error: Failed to create the shared library. Run 'printErrors()' to see the compilation errors.

I have attached the model code, which should be reproducible.

Thanks so very much!
Max

On Saturday, March 2, 2024 at 10:31:40 AM UTC-6 Perry de Valpine wrote:
> Hi Max,
> I actually don't see any errors there. Those are warnings that turn out to be harmless.  It is voluminous and alarming at first, but there's not much we can do about it. They come from the Eigen linear algebra package that we use. Eigen actually has a file in its source code called "DisableStupidWarnings.h" that uses C++ #pragma (pre-processor) statements do disable these warnings, but CRAN policy disallows disabling of C++ warnings in this way and scans code to catch violations of its policy, so we have to let the warning fly at you (if you have showCompilerOutput=TRUE). In general it is difficult to manage C++ compiler warnings because users may be running many variants of C++ compilers and configurations. That's why by default the C++ compiler output is not shown by compileNimble. If you are getting output that shows errors (typically with the word "error"), please send a reproducible example. Thanks and HTH.
> Perry

> > > Version 1.1.0, just released last week, should substantially smooth out the process of using nimbleHMC for models with discrete distributions. In particular, automatic differentiation (AD) can be used in a wider range of  models, including models with stochastic indexing, discrete latent states, and CAR distributions. Support for AD for these models means that HMC sampling and Laplace approximation can be used, although of course HMC samplers can only be assigned to nodes following continuous distributions. In addition, version 1.1.0 now allows distributions and functions (whether user-defined or built-in) that lack AD support (such as dinterval, dconstraint, and truncated distributions) to be used and compiled in AD-enabled models. The added flexibility increases the range of models in which one can use AD methods (HMC or Laplace) on some parts of a model and other samplers or methods on other parts.

> Hi Frédéric,

> > I met another issue while using buildLaplace (catually: just before): this is that derivatives cannont be calculated on some functions in the Nimble code. In the specific case I met, this was strange because the function was pnorm which is differentiable.
> >
> > Here is a (maybe silly) code to replicate the issue:
> >
> >
> >
> > library(nimble)
> >
> > pumpCode <- nimbleCode({
> >   for (i in 1:N){
> >     theta[i] ~ dnorm(alpha,exp(beta))
> >
> >     lambda[i] <- pnorm(0,theta[i],2.0)
> >
> >     #x[i] ~ dpois(4.0) # does not work
> >

> >
> >   }
> >
> >   #alpha ~ dexp(1.0)
> >
> >   #beta ~ dgamma(0.1, 1.0)
> >
> > alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0)
> >
> >   beta ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0)
> >
> >
> >
> > })
> >
> >
> >
> > pumpConsts <- list(N = 10, t = c(94.3, 15.7, 62.9, 126, 5.24, 31.4, 1.05, 1.05, 2.1, 10.5))
> >
> >
> >
> > set.seed(1)
> >
> >
> >
> > pumpData <- list(x = rbinom(10,1,0.5))
> >
> >
> >
> > pumpInits <- list(alpha = 0.1, beta = 0.1, theta = rep(0.1, pumpConsts$N))
> >
> >
> >
> > pump <- nimbleModel(code = pumpCode, name = "pump", constants = pumpConsts,
> >                     data = pumpData, inits = pumpInits, buildDerivs = TRUE)

> >
> > I then get the message:
> >
> > [Warning] function pnorm is not supported for derivatives.
> > This model will not compile. ...
> >
> >
> > Is it planned to incorporate more functions in the derivative capabilities of nimble/buildLapalace?
> >
> >
> > Sincerely,
> >
> >
> > Frédéric

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have just updated to nimbleHMC version 0.2.1 (in linux) (and 0.2.0 in windows) and got a no assignation "error" wheras with the same code in previous versions of addHMC I did not.

To make it replicabvle I have checked I met the same problem with the simple code given with the help of addHMC and such is the case. Here is the code:

code <- nimbleCode({

    b0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)

    b1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)

    sigma ~ dunif(0, 10000)

    for(i in 1:N) {

        mu[i] <- b0 + b1 * x[i]

        y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma)

    }

})

N <- 10

constants <- list(N = N, x = 1:N)

data <- list(y = 1:N)

inits <- list(b0 = 1, b1 = 0.1, sigma = 1)

messages.body_plain:
Frédéric, thanks your use of the nimbleHMC package, and also raising this issue.

Indeed, in the most recent update to nimbleHMC, some changes were made to increase consistency between the nimble MCMC package functions (such as configureMCMC and addSampler), and the nimbleHMC package functions (in particular, addHMC).  In doing so, the example appearing in the addHMC documentation appears to have fallen out-of-date.  Also you're correct, there is a small change to how addHMC operates, which I'll describe below.

The addHMC function is used to add an HMC sampler to an existing MCMC configuration object, where the HMC sampler will operate on one-or-more model nodes which are specified using the "target" argument to addHMC.  Therefore, the arguments to addHMC are (1) an MCMC configuration object, and (2) a specification of one-or-more model nodes.  If no "target" argument is specified, which is the default value, for example:

addHMC(conf)

then no HMC sampler is added to the "conf" object.  Yes, this is a change from the previous behavior, where omitting the "target" argument added an HMC sampler operating on *all* model nodes.  This change was made to be consistent with the addSampler method from the nimble package, and also because the behavior of creating an MCMC configuration with an HMC sampler operating on *all* model nodes is more directly accomplished using configureHMC:

conf <- configureHMC(model)

Accordingly, with this change, the example code you cited using addHMC should rather appear as:

nimbleHMC::addHMC(conf, target = c("b0", "b1"))    ## for example

I'll go ahead and update the example code in a not-too-distant update to nimbleHMC, and also improve the documentation for the "target" argument to addHMC, to make this more clear.

Does this make sense?  Please let me know if anything here is unclear, or I can help further.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: help with marginal WAIC w/ grouping
messages.subject_clean: help with marginal WAIC w/ grouping
messages.body_plain:
Hi Max,

In this case by virtue of each history being a (single) multivariate node, things are already grouped, with each multivariate node having a single likelihood value, and there should not be a need to specify groups (which is a way of combining *multiple* nodes and treating as a single contribution to WAIC). Also since `dHMM` has already marginalized over the latent states, one wouldn't explicitly ask for marginal WAIC. You're already getting a marginal WAIC based on your model specification.

As a side note, if instead one had a model in which `z` were explicitly in the model, one would have `z` (not `y` -- these are the observed nodes not the latent nodes) as the `marginalizeNodes`.  (and note "marginalizeNodes" not "MarginalizeNodes")

Similarly for `marr`, each row is a (single) multivariate node so already grouped and you shouldn't need to specify groups.

Let me know if that doesn't make sense or you have further questions.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Max,
Thanks for this. Yes, I reproduced this as well.
The problem is that the stochastic indexing in the dcat with derivatives enabled is not working for this case. Let me explain a little and give you a workaround. We'll try to extend AD to cover this in the future.
Here's the explanation. Doing AD correctly with stochastic indexing is actually surprisingly tricky. That's because the AD system (using CppAD) tracks (or records) all calculations in a model (or part of a model) and then reuses them forwards and backwards for derivatives, essentially for implementing the chain rule of calculus. When there is a stochastic index, the pathway of calculations may change. So this seemingly innocuous aspect of a model really complicates any system that manages calculations as a static graph or tree structure. One way or another, all elements rather than just a single element need to be included in the graph. (This is true in basic nimble models as well (but is more thoroughly implemented than for AD) and always introduces more computation.) Some cases now work, but the one if your code doesn't.
Here's the workaround. Stochastic indexing does work one by one. So one can write a nimbleFunction to provide a special flavor of dcat that constructs the vector TPM[t-1,z[i,t-1],1:10] (for example) one by one and then calls the dcat distribution. That's easy enough and is dmycat in the attached code. Then one wants the categorical sampler to work, but that needs tweaking to determine how many categories are available and to disable an error-trap that gets in the way. I copied the sampler_categorical source code and made these modifications. And finally one needs a little code to assign this tweaked sampler to the dmycat nodes, which I've also done.
The modified model code looks like
      z[i,t] ~ dmycat(TPM[t-1, 1:10, 1:10], z[i,t-1]) # replaces dcat(TPM[t-1,z[i,t-1],1:10])
      y[i,t] ~ dmycat(OPM[i, 1:10, 1:10], z[i, t]).     # replaced dcat(OPM[i,z[i,t],1:10])
The other changes are a bit longer and are in the attached file. The model and MCMC build and compile on my system. I didn't investigate further whether they work well or not.
Let me know how it goes.
Perry

> > > > > Version 1.1.0, just released last week, should substantially smooth out the process of using nimbleHMC for models with discrete distributions. In particular, automatic differentiation (AD) can be used in a wider range of  models, including models with stochastic indexing, discrete latent states, and CAR distributions. Support for AD for these models means that HMC sampling and Laplace approximation can be used, although of course HMC samplers can only be assigned to nodes following continuous distributions. In addition, version 1.1.0 now allows distributions and functions (whether user-defined or built-in) that lack AD support (such as dinterval, dconstraint, and truncated distributions) to be used and compiled in AD-enabled models. The added flexibility increases the range of models in which one can use AD methods (HMC or Laplace) on some parts of a model and other samplers or methods on other parts.
> > > > >
> > > > > We've updated this section <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-AD.html#what-operations-are-and-arent-supported-for-ad> of the manual to try to be clear about what is and is not supported by AD and implications for derivative-based methods such as HMC.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am unsure this is a new request but I did not find the information in the Nimble manual nor in this list (searching with "parameter order", "parameters order" or "order of parameters").

I would like to take some of the partameters out of an MCMC from nimble and feed them into a call to a Nimble function (in my case: close to what is done with Cglmm_laplace$calcLaplace in the Nimble manual).

Yet it is unclear for me in which order should the parameters feed the $calcLaplace function all the more so that I have logProb or intermediate nodes in my output. Is there a place in the manual or in the help files where this is explained?

Thanks very much in adavance.

All the best,

Frédéric

messages.body_plain:
Hi Frédéric,

I may not be fully following your question. Are you asking about how to get the order of parameter nodes inside the buildLaplace function? If you provide an input for the paramNodes argument of the function, the order will be the same as what has been provided. If you let the function decide what should be regarded as parameters (by default top-level stochastic nodes excluding any posterior predictive nodes), then you can take a look at what has been included via the method $getNodeNamesVec(returnParams = TRUE). Similarly you can take a look at random effects nodes used in Laplace you can do $getNodeNamesVec(returnParams = FALSE). The getNodeNamesVec method is introduced in the help page of buildLaplace. Please let us know if this is what you are looking for.

Best wishes,
Wei

messages.subject_clean: Reproducibility question
messages.body_plain:
Hi All

I have been asked about how to get reproducibility with Nimble. I am not familiar with how setting seeds works in Nimble.

I assumed, following suggestions, that if you setSeed=number within the runMCMC function

then the results should be reproducible.

My question is ‘How close should the results be when the seed is the same for the same run?

Below is some results of running a spatial convolution model on some health data .

I ran the following:

On R I set.seed= 123987001 and then ran the following

samples1<-runMCMC(CCONVMCMC,niter=niter,nburnin=10000,nchains=1,summary=TRUE,WAIC=TRUE,setSeed=123987001)

samples1$WAIC

samples2<-runMCMC(CCONVMCMC,niter=niter,nburnin=10000,nchains=1,summary=TRUE,WAIC=TRUE,setSeed=123987001)

samples2$WAIC

The results of these two calls were:

samples1$WAIC

nimbleList object of type waicNimbleList

Field "WAIC":

[1] 318.6866

Field "lppd":

[1] -142.6599

Field "pWAIC":

[1] 16.68338

samples2$WAIC

nimbleList object of type waicNimbleList

Field "WAIC":

[1] 316.6697

Field "lppd":

[1] -142.3672

Field "pWAIC":

[1] 15.96761

The lppd is virtually the same but the variance penalty differs. There are also different numbers of warnings about pWAIC >0.4

Any suggestions about how to guarantee reproducibility or assurance that this is reproducibility welcome.

Best

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am currently running a simple ODE as part of model by wrapping a deSolve function into a nimbleRcall(). However, even with a very simple version of the ODE and very few observations being used the model is taking an exorbitant amount of time to run (110 seconds for 100 iterations). The project I am currently working on is invested in using nimble and having an ODE as part of this model we are working on. However, the amount of time that a simple version of this model is taking is very daunting. We (my PI) has experience using Rcpp functions and C++ libraries and we are wondering if there is a way to leverage these within a nimble model. For example, could we use a function from the C++ "boost" library within the nimbleModel to lessen the overhead time from moving back and forth between C++ and R?

Thanks for any info on this.
Colton

messages.body_plain:
Hi Colton,
For quick answers:
1. Look at nimbleExternalCall. It is somewhat rudimentary but is designed to let you call C/C++ code directly (from compiled nimble code), without going through the R interpreter. But to use Rcpp, you may have to code the C++ and create the #includes etc yourself and rely less on Rcpp's slickness (e.g. sourceCpp) directly from R. You need to have access to both the .o and .h files.
2. I am not a deSolve expert but I think it wraps layers of R processing around a call to a C++ internal that does the actual integration. It may be the case that all the time in the R interpreter is what is so costly. If nimbleExternalCall is too clunky, you could do the following: Use Rcpp completely independently of nimble, so that you have an R function (created by Rcpp) that calls directly to compiled code to compute what you want. Then call that function via a nimbleRcall. The overhead for the nimbleRcall should be much less (but not nothing) if you're not spending time executing R other than calling back into compiled code.
I'm happy to help look at details or sketch ideas if you start exploring one of these.
HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,
In theory setting the same seed should produce identical results. My first guess is that the model is not in identical state at the start of each run and that explains why the outputs are not identical. You could recreate the model state by doing something like the following, assuming Cmodel is the compiled model.

# before first run
savedVars <- list()
for(var in Cmodel$getVarNames()) {
 savedVars[[var]] <- Cmodel[[var]]
}

# before second run
for(var in Cmodel$getVarNames()) {
 Cmodel[[var]] <- savedVars[[var]]
}

HTH
Perry

messages.subject: Re: Laplace approximation within MCMC
messages.subject_clean: Laplace approximation within MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel,

just for sharing (and checking): I propose the following function when what we specify are the random effects on which to marginalize: is this OK?

llFun_Laplace <- nimbleFunction(
    setup = function(model, RENodes) {
        laplace <- buildLaplace(model, randomEffectsNodes=RENodes)
paramNodes<-laplace$getNodeNamesVec(returnParams = TRUE)

    },
    run = function() {
        paramValues <- values(model, paramNodes)
        ll <- laplace$calcLaplace(paramValues)
        returnType(double())
        return(ll)
    }
)

Sincerely,

Frédéric

Le samedi 17 juin 2023 à 07:53:04 UTC+2, frederic....@gmail.com a écrit :
> Thank you very much Daniel for both the solution (it works!) and the explanation. Will be useful for others.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Frédéric
>
> Le vendredi 16 juin 2023 à 21:46:02 UTC+2, Daniel Turek a écrit :
> > Frédéric, great that you're trying out the new functionality.  Give it a try using the modified code, below.  The main change is that you needed to define a custom nimbleFunction to serve the role of the llFunction for the RW_llFunction_block sampler.  I defined the nimbleFunction as llFun_Laplace, and the specialized instance of it (specialized to the model, and the {alpha, beta} parameters) is called llFun.  This custom function stores new values of alpha and beta into the model, executes the Laplace approximation (calcLaplace method), then returns the (approximate) marginal log-likelihood of alpha and beta.
> >
> > The code below also removes the default (conjugate) samplers which are assigned to the theta[] elements, since those will be marginalized over in the Laplace approximation.
> >
> > The code also uses the RW_llFunction_block sampler (rather than the RW_llFunction sampler, as you had), to jointly update both {alpha, beta} together.  I believe that is the necessary approach for the Laplace in MCMC for this model, since {alpha, beta} together, jointly, define the prior distribution for the theta[] elements which are integrated out.
> >
> > But, hopefully / likely others will have better ideas and suggestions for you, as well.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> > pump <- nimbleModel(code = pumpCode, name = "pump", constants = pumpConsts, data = pumpData, inits = pumpInits, buildDerivs = TRUE)
> >
> > Cpump <- compileNimble(pump)
> >
> >
> > Confpump<-configureMCMC(pump, thin =10, monitors = c("alpha","beta"))
> >
> > Confpump$removeSamplers(c("alpha","beta","theta"))
> >
> > llFun_Laplace <- nimbleFunction(
> >     setup = function(model, paramNodes) {
> >         laplace <- buildLaplace(model, paramNodes)
> >     },
> >     run = function() {
> >         paramValues <- values(model, paramNodes)
> >         ll <- laplace$calcLaplace(paramValues)
> >         returnType(double())
> >         return(ll)
> >     }
> > )
> >
> > llFun <- llFun_Laplace(pump, paramNodes = c("alpha", "beta"))
> >
> > Confpump$addSampler(target = c("alpha", "beta"),
> >                     type = 'RW_llFunction_block',
> >                     control = list(llFunction = llFun, includesTarget = FALSE))
> >
> >
> > ModelMCMCpump <- nimble::buildMCMC(Confpump)
> >
> > CModelMCMCpump <- nimble::compileNimble(ModelMCMCpump, project =Cpump)
> >
> > samples <- runMCMC(CModelMCMCpump, 1000)
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Jun 16, 2023 at 11:31 AM frederic....@gmail.com <frederic....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Dear all,
> > >
> > > I would like to test the use of the Laplace approximation to marginalize the log posterior density within a MCMC - as I have seen during ISEC 2022 conference. I have tried to do it based on the example in the help file for the function buildLaplace. But here weems to be an error just at the end.

messages.body_plain:
Frédéric, great that you're making progress on this.  Yes, I think that code will work as you intend, I'll only add that when you provide the randomEffectsNodes argument, this will (in some sense) affect what the parameter nodes are, in that the parameter nodes will now be defined as the parent nodes (parameters) of the randomEffectsNodes - in contrast to the otherwise default set of parameter nodes, being the model's top-level stochastic nodes.  In most cases this designation should logically be what you want, but I wanted to highlight the difference.

Also I should note that Wei is the guru on the Laplace functionality, and he will be more qualified to give a complete answer.

Cheers!
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Daniel has already explained this well. One more point I want to add here is that since you are using this within MCMC then you should be careful about setting up the RW_llFunction/RW_llFunction_block samplers. More specifically, when you specify particular random effects nodes to integrate out, their stochastic parent nodes (i.e. paramNodes within Laplace) need to be assigned with a RW_llFunction/RW_llFunction_block sampler for MCMC. However, sometimes the llFun_Laplace function you write here does not include all the log-likelihood needed for the paramNodes, i.e. they may have other stochastic dependencies that are not inside the random effects nodes you specified. Then you need to add the log-likelihood component from those nodes into the custom log-likelihood calculation like this:
ll <- laplace$calcLaplace(paramValues) + model$calculate(extraDepsofParams)
Actually, we have used the pump example to demonstrate this kind of scenario. Please take a look at the code given here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/Laplace-examples/pump/pumpNimble.R And by the way in the same place, we have some other Laplace examples.

Hope this helps, and we are happy to discuss any questions you may have.

Cheers,
Wei

On Wednesday, February 14, 2024 at 2:10:13 PM UTC-8 Wei Zhang wrote:
> Arjun, the way you set up the data and missing values is fine. The thing that does not make sense is explained in more detail below.
>
> In your simulated fl data, the 1st row is:  NA, 174, 181, NA, 182, NA ,188. This means the 1st individual is first captured on the 2nd occasion. So, we need to model the observed difference between the 2nd and 3rd occasions, i.e. 7 (=181-174), using the gamma distribution. Then we need to use delta[1, 1] ~ dgamma(a, b) for the difference between the 3rd and 4th occasions, and let the missing fl[1, 4] <- fl[1, 3] + delta[1, 1]. Now we need to model the next revolution, i.e. fl[1,5] - fl[1,4] using the gamma dist. Next is delta[1,2] ~ dgamma(a, b) for the missing value on occasion 6, etc. The annoying thing is that we cannot declare something like fl[1, 5] - fl[1, 4] ~ dgamma(a, b) in nimble model code. I may be wrong but I do not have a better way to handle this than the following two:
>

On Wednesday, March 6, 2024 at 8:04:37 PM UTC-6 Perry de Valpine wrote:
> Hi Max,
> Thanks for this. Yes, I reproduced this as well.
> The problem is that the stochastic indexing in the dcat with derivatives enabled is not working for this case. Let me explain a little and give you a workaround. We'll try to extend AD to cover this in the future.
> Here's the explanation. Doing AD correctly with stochastic indexing is actually surprisingly tricky. That's because the AD system (using CppAD) tracks (or records) all calculations in a model (or part of a model) and then reuses them forwards and backwards for derivatives, essentially for implementing the chain rule of calculus. When there is a stochastic index, the pathway of calculations may change. So this seemingly innocuous aspect of a model really complicates any system that manages calculations as a static graph or tree structure. One way or another, all elements rather than just a single element need to be included in the graph. (This is true in basic nimble models as well (but is more thoroughly implemented than for AD) and always introduces more computation.) Some cases now work, but the one if your code doesn't.
> Here's the workaround. Stochastic indexing does work one by one. So one can write a nimbleFunction to provide a special flavor of dcat that constructs the vector TPM[t-1,z[i,t-1],1:10] (for example) one by one and then calls the dcat distribution. That's easy enough and is dmycat in the attached code. Then one wants the categorical sampler to work, but that needs tweaking to determine how many categories are available and to disable an error-trap that gets in the way. I copied the sampler_categorical source code and made these modifications. And finally one needs a little code to assign this tweaked sampler to the dmycat nodes, which I've also done.
> The modified model code looks like
>       z[i,t] ~ dmycat(TPM[t-1, 1:10, 1:10], z[i,t-1]) # replaces dcat(TPM[t-1,z[i,t-1],1:10])
>       y[i,t] ~ dmycat(OPM[i, 1:10, 1:10], z[i, t]).     # replaced dcat(OPM[i,z[i,t],1:10])
> The other changes are a bit longer and are in the attached file. The model and MCMC build and compile on my system. I didn't investigate further whether they work well or not.
> Let me know how it goes.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all "nimbleans",

I have an autoregressive model with data dependent on time.
I would like to calculate a summary statistic for each time point, t, based only on the data and the posterior samples until time point t-1. After each calculation of the statistic I would like to add a new data point for t+1.
Does someone knows if it is possible to code something like that on the fly, or we have to rerun the model, add a new data point, each time we want to make a new posterior prediction?

Thanks in advance

Cheers
Rui

Dear all,

I am reopening this discussion as I actually meet a series of problems using buildLalpace. My (three) problems are the following ones - with the version 1.0.1 of Nimble in Windows and 1.1.0 on Linux:
     (i) when part of the data Likelihood is not related to the random effects being integrated out, they seem not to be included in the calculation of the likelihood in $calcLaplace: here are two codes that should give the same results but that do not, due to this "problem". I am unsure this is a problem. At least it should be mentioned in the Nimble help what is included in calcLaplace. Note that I have to run these two codes in different R sessions due to the problem reported in point (ii) below. :

library(nimble)

pumpCode <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:N){

    theta[i] ~ dnorm(alpha,exp(beta))

    lambda[i] <- theta[i] * t[i]

    #x[i] ~ dpois(4.0) # does not work

x[i] ~ dpois(0*lambda[i]+4.0)

x2[i] ~ dpois(4.0)

  }

  #alpha ~ dexp(1.0)

  #beta ~ dgamma(0.1, 1.0)

alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0)

  beta ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0)

})

pumpConsts <- list(N = 10, t = c(94.3, 15.7, 62.9, 126, 5.24, 31.4, 1.05, 1.05, 2.1, 10.5))

pumpData <- list(x = c(5, 1, 5, 14, 3, 19, 1, 1, 4, 22), x2 = c(5, 1, 5, 14, 3, 19, 1, 1, 4, 22))

pumpInits <- list(alpha = 0.1, beta = 0.1, theta = rep(0.1, pumpConsts$N))

pump <- nimbleModel(code = pumpCode, name = "pump", constants = pumpConsts,
                    data = pumpData, inits = pumpInits, buildDerivs = TRUE)

pumpLaplace <- buildLaplace(pump, randomEffectsNodes = "theta")

CpumpLaplace <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, project = compileNimble(pump))

CpumpLaplace$calcLaplace(c(1,1))

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

another issue I have with the buildLaplace function is when some of the random effects that are marginalized on correspond to no data. This may seem strange to you but it may be of use for example to calculate marginalized looIC (which is my case). Here is a replicable example: two models: in the first one observed data correspond to each of the levels of the random effect; in the second one, for theta[2] there is no related observation and the result of $calcLaplace is Infinity:

library(nimble)

pumpCode <- nimbleCode({

for (i in 1:2){ theta[i] ~ dnorm(alpha,exp(beta))}

for (j in 1:5) { thetab[j] ~ dnorm(0,1)}

  for (i in 1:2){

for (j in 1:5) {

    lambda[5*(i-1)+j] <- exp(theta[i]) * t[i]*exp(thetab[j])

    #x[i] ~ dpois(4.0) # does not work

x[5*(i-1)+j] ~ dpois(0*lambda[5*(i-1)+j]+4.0)

  }}

  #alpha ~ dexp(1.0)

  #beta ~ dgamma(0.1, 1.0)

alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0)

  beta ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0)

})

pumpConsts <- list(N = 10, t = c(94.3, 15.7, 62.9, 126, 5.24, 31.4, 1.05, 1.05, 2.1, 10.5))

pumpData <- list(x = c(5, 1, 5, 14, 3, 19, 1, 1, 4, 22))

pumpInits <- list(alpha = 0.1, beta = 0.1, theta = rep(0.1, pumpConsts$N))

pump <- nimbleModel(code = pumpCode, name = "pump", constants = pumpConsts,
                    data = pumpData, inits = pumpInits, buildDerivs = TRUE)

pumpLaplace <- buildLaplace(pump, randomEffectsNodes = "theta")

CpumpLaplace <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, project = compileNimble(pump))

CpumpLaplace$calcLaplace(c(1,1,0,0,0,0,0))

# -63.57501 (OK)

library(nimble)

pumpCode <- nimbleCode({

for (i in 1:2){ theta[i] ~ dnorm(alpha,exp(beta))}

for (j in 1:5) { thetab[j] ~ dnorm(0,1)}

  for (i in 1:1){

for (j in 1:5) {

    lambda[5*(i-1)+j] <- exp(theta[i]) * t[i]*exp(thetab[j])

    #x[i] ~ dpois(4.0) # does not work

x[5*(i-1)+j] ~ dpois(0*lambda[5*(i-1)+j]+4.0)

  }}

  #alpha ~ dexp(1.0)

  #beta ~ dgamma(0.1, 1.0)

alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0)

> > > > > > Here is what I believe is happening. buildLaplace, by default, uses the model graph (what depends on what) to decide what should be treated as a random effect to integrate over. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(0*lambda[i]+4.0)there is a graph dependency that x[i] depends on lambda[i] (even though we humans can see it is always multiplied by 0), so theta[i] (on which lambda[i] depends deterministically) can be determined to be a random effect. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(4.0)nimble believes (correctly) that there is no dependency from theta-->lambda-->x, and so theta is not a random effect.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

my last problem at the moment with buildLaplace - but for which I cannot produce a replicable example - is that the names of active parameters produced with the  $getNodeNamesVec(returnParams = TRUE) of the compiled model does not correspond well (in terms of number of parametrs) to what is required by $calcLaplace. In my specific case I can correct for this but may indicate a problem somewhere in the code.

Sincerely,

Frédéric Gosselin

Le vendredi 8 mars 2024 à 12:49:42 UTC+1, Wei Zhang a écrit :
> Daniel has already explained this well. One more point I want to add here is that since you are using this within MCMC then you should be careful about setting up the RW_llFunction/RW_llFunction_block samplers. More specifically, when you specify particular random effects nodes to integrate out, their stochastic parent nodes (i.e. paramNodes within Laplace) need to be assigned with a RW_llFunction/RW_llFunction_block sampler for MCMC. However, sometimes the llFun_Laplace function you write here does not include all the log-likelihood needed for the paramNodes, i.e. they may have other stochastic dependencies that are not inside the random effects nodes you specified. Then you need to add the log-likelihood component from those nodes into the custom log-likelihood calculation like this:
> ll <- laplace$calcLaplace(paramValues) + model$calculate(extraDepsofParams)
> Actually, we have used the pump example to demonstrate this kind of scenario. Please take a look at the code given here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/Laplace-examples/pump/pumpNimble.R And by the way in the same place, we have some other Laplace examples.
>
> Hope this helps, and we are happy to discuss any questions you may have.
>
> Cheers,
> Wei

In most cases this designation should logically be what you want, but I wanted to highlight the difference.

> > > > > Frédéric, great that you're trying out the new functionality.  Give it a try using the modified code, below.  The main change is that you needed to define a custom nimbleFunction to serve the role of the llFunction for the RW_llFunction_block sampler.  I defined the nimbleFunction as llFun_Laplace, and the specialized instance of it (specialized to the model, and the {alpha, beta} parameters) is called llFun.  This custom function stores new values of alpha and beta into the model, executes the Laplace approximation (calcLaplace method), then returns the (approximate) marginal log-likelihood of alpha and beta.
> > > > >
> > > > > The code below also removes the default (conjugate) samplers which are assigned to the theta[] elements, since those will be marginalized over in the Laplace approximation.
> > > > >
> > > > > The code also uses the RW_llFunction_block sampler (rather than the RW_llFunction sampler, as you had), to jointly update both {alpha, beta} together.  I believe that is the necessary approach for the Laplace in MCMC for this model, since {alpha, beta} together, jointly, define the prior distribution for the theta[] elements which are integrated out.
> > > > >
> > > > > But, hopefully / likely others will have better ideas and suggestions for you, as well.
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: one step-ahead prediction
messages.subject_clean: one step-ahead prediction
messages.body_plain:
Rui, good question.  Yes, this sort of thing is certainly possible, although it might require a little bit of knowledge and manipulation of the model and MCMC.  For example, you could create a model with T steps in the time series, and also create an MCMC which has the ability to sample all T steps.  But, by changing values in the model and/or MCMC samplers, you could "turn off" parts of the model or the MCMC.  Thus, initially, only treat the model as having t0 < T time steps, make a prediction for t0+1, then manipulate the model to add this new "data point" to the model.  The values (and designation of data) in the model can be manipulated using functions such as:

model$values(node) <- new_value
model$setData(...)
model$resetData(...)

Manipulating (turning off parts of) the MCMC would require a little more understanding of the inner-workings of MCMC samplers, but is certainly also possible.

I guess in summary: if you have a somewhat large model, and want to do this procedure for some number of time steps, then the approach I described above (while requiring some upfront effort to get working) will pay off in the end.  However, if your model is not terribly large, and you don't need to repeat this procedure for very many additional time steps, then it would probably be easier and faster overall to just rebuild new models (with progressively additional data), and refit them anew.

Let me know if you'd like to discuss this more.

Cheers,
Daniel

I've been writing a JS model (with the aim to add additional covariates for survival).
However, I already to run into a problem with the simplified model.

The model runs but the estimated survival and detection probabilities are still off from the simulated dataset.

Additionally, I receive the following messages:
warning: logProb of data node y[26, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[92, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[117, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[136, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[187, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[208, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[307, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[328, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[354, 1]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[1, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[49, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[72, 2]: logProb is -Inf. warning: logProb of data node y[92, 2]: logProb is -Inf.

and so on..
Which corresponds to the first captures (y[,]=1).

I suspect there is an issue with how I have defined the Dirichlet distribution for entry probabilities.

If someone would be willing to help, I would be really great full!
I've attached the code for both the model and the simulated dataset in case anyone wants to take a look.

Thanks in advance,
Shaquille

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the questions and reports, Frédéric. I will try to address them in order.

1. Your question about why using
x[i] ~ dpois(4.0)
gives results you didn't expect, and what is documented.

I feel I am not following the question because it looks the same or similar to an earlier question we responded to. nimbleModel creates a graph of relationships among variables. This declaration for x[i] says it has no parent nodes, so the graph may not be what you think it would be. It is correct from the default graphical model perspective that there is nothing to integrate over here, as x[i] is structurally a top-level node or parameter and not a random effect or latent state. The documentation for buildLaplace says that you can call setupMargNodes directly to see how nodes will be handled based on your inputs. The documentation for setupMargNodes is complicated because there are a variety of complicated cases that arise. Again, I may have become lost by the multiple questions so please clarify if I am missing it. You may be asking about parts of the model that should be (or you want to be) included in the likelihood but simply are unrelated to what is being marginalized. Those are called "calcNodesOther" in Laplace, and you can see what setupMargNodes thinks they are, and you can provide them if the default isn't what you want. In your example I am not seeing what you think should be happening, as the x[i] are declared as a set of stand-alone (in effect, predictive) nodes.

2. Your report about crashes when creating and then recreating a model and Laplace algorithm in the same R session: There is a known issue here and it is something we'll try to fix. However I've normally seen that if you rebuild the model (nimbleModel) and recompile it, and then build the Laplace and compile it, I don't see crashes. One thing I see in your code that is unusual to me is:
CpumpLaplace <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, project = compileNimble(pump)). It makes sense but I would comment that you can do:
CompiledBoth <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, pump) and then you'll get a list of the two compiled interface objects.

3. Thanks for the report about (if I follow) the length of the node names returned not matching the length of the parameter input to calcLaplace. I will file an issue to look at that.

Perry

> > > > > > > > Here is what I believe is happening. buildLaplace, by default, uses the model graph (what depends on what) to decide what should be treated as a random effect to integrate over. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(0*lambda[i]+4.0)there is a graph dependency that x[i] depends on lambda[i] (even though we humans can see it is always multiplied by 0), so theta[i] (on which lambda[i] depends deterministically) can be determined to be a random effect. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(4.0)nimble believes (correctly) that there is no dependency from theta-->lambda-->x, and so theta is not a random effect.

P.S. Something else to try on #2 would be to remove the name argument to nimbleModel. Please let us know if that seems to help.

On Mon, Mar 18, 2024 at 9:39 AM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Thanks for the questions and reports, Frédéric. I will try to address them in order.
>
> 1. Your question about why using
> x[i] ~ dpois(4.0)
> gives results you didn't expect, and what is documented.
>
> I feel I am not following the question because it looks the same or similar to an earlier question we responded to. nimbleModel creates a graph of relationships among variables. This declaration for x[i] says it has no parent nodes, so the graph may not be what you think it would be. It is correct from the default graphical model perspective that there is nothing to integrate over here, as x[i] is structurally a top-level node or parameter and not a random effect or latent state. The documentation for buildLaplace says that you can call setupMargNodes directly to see how nodes will be handled based on your inputs. The documentation for setupMargNodes is complicated because there are a variety of complicated cases that arise. Again, I may have become lost by the multiple questions so please clarify if I am missing it. You may be asking about parts of the model that should be (or you want to be) included in the likelihood but simply are unrelated to what is being marginalized. Those are called "calcNodesOther" in Laplace, and you can see what setupMargNodes thinks they are, and you can provide them if the default isn't what you want. In your example I am not seeing what you think should be happening, as the x[i] are declared as a set of stand-alone (in effect, predictive) nodes.
>
> 2. Your report about crashes when creating and then recreating a model and Laplace algorithm in the same R session: There is a known issue here and it is something we'll try to fix. However I've normally seen that if you rebuild the model (nimbleModel) and recompile it, and then build the Laplace and compile it, I don't see crashes. One thing I see in your code that is unusual to me is:
> CpumpLaplace <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, project = compileNimble(pump)). It makes sense but I would comment that you can do:
> CompiledBoth <- compileNimble(pumpLaplace, pump) and then you'll get a list of the two compiled interface objects.
>
> 3. Thanks for the report about (if I follow) the length of the node names returned not matching the length of the parameter input to calcLaplace. I will file an issue to look at that.
>
> Perry

> > > > > > > > > Here is what I believe is happening. buildLaplace, by default, uses the model graph (what depends on what) to decide what should be treated as a random effect to integrate over. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(0*lambda[i]+4.0)there is a graph dependency that x[i] depends on lambda[i] (even though we humans can see it is always multiplied by 0), so theta[i] (on which lambda[i] depends deterministically) can be determined to be a random effect. When you use x[i] ~ dpois(4.0)nimble believes (correctly) that there is no dependency from theta-->lambda-->x, and so theta is not a random effect.

> > > > > > > > > You can see the relevant sets of (default) nodes by
> > > > > > > > > setupMargNodes(pump, c('alpha','beta'))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > There are other arguments to setupMargNodes and/or buildLaplace for fine-grained control, all the way up to specifying your choices of parameters, random effects, and calculation nodes.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Shaquille,
I ran your code and explored a bit. I think you will need to give more complete initial values. The initial values filled in by default using draws from the priors are resulting in impossible model states. For example, I got that y[159,2] is 1, but pcap[159, 2] is 0, which makes y[159,2]==1 impossible, resulting in a log probability of -Inf, which will often result in mayhem and meaningless results. This appears to be happening in other places too. It's not uncommon that in demographic models one can get impossible initial states (e.g. going from dead to alive) unless care is taken to avoid that. Below is some of my code to investigate. You might find our user manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> helpful if you haven't explored it yet. HTH.
Perry

# Following nimbleModel:
Build.model$calculate() # This is the same as calculate=TRUE
# to see if everything is initialized: no.
# We get
#Error in if (x1 == x2) 1 else 0 : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
# So let's catch the error and inspect
options(error = recover)
Build.model$calculate()
# I select the last evaluation frame and see the
# error is from nimEquals,
# which appears only in
# bij[i,j] <- equals(alive[i,j-1],0)*equals(alive[i,j],1)
# The first argument ("x1") is NA
# Ok, maybe I didn't need to get that low-level.
# Let's see what values are in the model.
Build.model$alive
Build.model$notyetdead
Build.model$w
Biuld.model$psi
# everything is NA. The model is far from fully initialized.
# Ok, potentially not a problem.
# The next step is to
# see what happens when the MCMC tries to initialize such nodes
# with draws from the prior.
MCMC <- buildMCMC(Build.model)
# By running for 0 iterations, we get the initialization only,
# with no sampling.
MCMC$run(niter = 0)
# Notice I am running this uncompiled so we can error trap and
# investigate from R
# This generates lots of logProb errors, starting with
warning: logProb of data node y[159, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
# Let me look at that one.
Build.model$y[159,2] #
Build.model$calculate("y[159, 2]") # -Inf
Build.model$pcap[159, 2] # 0
Build.model$y[159, 2] # 1
Build.model$p[159, 2] # 0.1401046
Build.model$alive[159, 2] # 0
# Conclusion: This model has impossible states.
# Recommendation: Provide inits that start the model in a valid state.

messages.subject: how to get mid-posterior p-values when using a ones trick?
messages.subject_clean: how to get mid-posterior p-values when using a ones trick?
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I am implementing a generalized Poisson likelihood function using a “ones trick.” I can obtain the posterior distribution without trouble, and I can *almost* get an appropriate posterior predictive distribution and posterior predictive p-values for my variable of interest (z).

The problem is that to get the posterior predictive distribution for z using the ones trick, I have to specify that z is missing (I call this variable msgZ) and assign it a half-flat prior. The half-flat prior makes msgZ continuous, and in turn, the posterior predictive p-values are incorrect, since I have no way to construct a discrete mid-p-value. This causes the greatest problem when the observed count (z[i,j]) is 0, because the continuous posterior p-value is always 0; whereas, the discrete mid-p-value would not be.

Is there a way I can fix this problem without custom coding a generalized Poisson random number generator? (I’m terrified of the time it will take me to learn how to do that.) I’m copying my code below. The section of interest starts with “# POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE DISTRIBUTION”, but I thought the code that obtains the posterior might also be helpful, so you will see that first. Thank you! Rebecca

# GENERALIZED POISSON LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION

  for(i in 1:n){ # THERE ARE n SITES

    for (j in 1:g[i]){ # THERE ARE g[i] OBSERVATIONS PER SITE

      # x[i,j] IS A KNOWN MEASUREMENT, theta[i] IS A PARAMETER

      meanZ[i,j] <- x[i,j]*theta[i]

      # LOG LIKELIHOOD OF DATUM z[i,j]

      lfz[i,j] <- log(1-delta[i]) + log(meanZ[i,j]) +

        (z[i,j]-1)*log((1-delta[i])*meanZ[i,j] + delta[i]*z[i,j]) -

        (1-delta[i])*meanZ[i,j] - delta[i]*z[i,j]  -  lfactorial(z[i,j])

      prOnes[i,j] <- exp(lfz[i,j])/1000

      #OnesMat IS A MATRIX OF 1s (BUT PADDED WITH NAs)

      OnesMat[i,j] ~ dbern(prOnes[i,j])

    }

# PRIORS

    delta[i] <- 1 - 1/sqrt(alpha[i])

    theta[i] ~ dlnorm(mlog, taulog)

    alpha[i] ~ dunif(1,45)

  }

# HYPERPRIORS

  taulog<- (1/slog)^2

  slog <-  (log((sdv/mn)^2 + 1))^(1/2)

  mlog <-  log(mn) - (1/2)*log((sdv/mn)^2 + 1)

  mn ~ T(dnorm(0, sd=10), 0,)

  sdv ~ T(dnorm(0, sd=10), 0,)

  # POSTERIOR PREDICTIVE DISTRIBUTION

  for (i in 1:n){ # THERE ARE n SITES

    for (j in 1:g[i]){ # THERE ARE g[i] OBSERVATIONS PER SITE

      # LOG DENSITY FOR PPD

      lfzNew[i,j] <- log(1-delta[i]) + log(meanZ[i,j]) +

        (msgZ[i,j]-1)*log((1-delta[i])*meanZ[i,j] + delta[i]*msgZ[i,j]) -

        (1-delta[i])*meanZ[i,j] - delta[i]*msgZ[i,j]  -  lfactorial(msgZ[i,j])

      prOnesNew[i,j] <- exp(lfzNew[i,j])/1000

      # OnesMatNew IS A MATRIX OF 1s (BUT PADDED WITH NAs)

      OnesMatNew[i,j] ~ dbern(prOnesNew[i,j])

      # msgZ IS A MATRIX OF NAs

      msgZ[i,j] ~ dhalfflat()

      PostPvalZ[i,j] <- msgZ[i,j] <= z[i,j]

      }

 }

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rebecca,
I think I follow your question, although I haven't worked through your full code setup and might be missing something but want to reply quickly.
I haven't worked with the generalized Poisson, but what I see is that methods to draw from it are non-trivial. Maybe that is why you don't want to write it (or is the obstacle the nimbleFunction syntax etc.)?
One option would be to create a user-defined distribution where in the "r" function you call a function that is a nimbleRcall (i.e. returned from the function nimbleRcall) that calls a simulation function from the package RNGforGPD. You would incur some overhead for time spent in the R evaluator, but it seems like the easiest way to get what you want. Since it is posterior predictive, you might be able to do it separately after the MCMC sampling, unless it depends on many nodes that are not being monitored from the MCMC. (Or you could use monitors2 and thin2 to save a sparser sample of more nodes and then use those post-MCMC).
I am less confident I follow what you want as you've set things up. (Specifically, I am not sure what is the discrete mid-p-value?). One approach to making goodness-of-fit statistics from discrete situations is to make them continuous by sampling uniformly between integers (See DHARMa package). OTOH if what you need is to make z go from continuous to discrete, could you use round(x), floor(x) or ceiling(x)?
Perry

messages.subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: how to get mid-posterior p-values when using a ones trick?
messages.subject_clean: [EXTERNAL] Re: how to get mid-posterior p-values when using a ones trick?
messages.body_plain:
Thank you, as always Perry, for a prompt and helpful reply. Regarding mid posterior p-values, they are used when your data are discrete. For example, suppose I’m using a (plain vanilla) Poisson distribution, my datum is an integer-valued 0, and I generate an integer-valued 0 from my posterior predictive distribution. If I calculate a “regular” posterior p-value, I have

PostPvalZ <- Znew <= Z,

which always returns a 1, so my model never fits the datum, even though it should. If I use the mid-posterior p-value, then I have

PostPvalZ <- (Znew < Z) + (1/2)*(Znew == Z),

which returns a 0.5, so my datum (which is 0), fits my posterior predicted point (which is 0). (For the interest of the community, a reference is p 153 of Gelman’s Bayesian Data Analysis 3rd edition.)

Back to my nimble code for a generalized Poisson distribution, because of the half-flat prior being continuous, my posterior predictive distribution is a continuous version of the generalized Poisson distribution…..and I’m afraid I don’t really even know what that means, since it is supposed to be a discrete distribution. With regard to the posterior p-values (which cannot be computed as mid-p-values because the posterior predictive distribution is continuous, not discrete, thus the term (1/2)*(Znew == Z) always returns a 0), they really aren’t correct.

I thought about rounding the values generated from the PPD, but I’m just not sure if that’s ok. Am I even generating values from a generalized Poisson distribution if the values I generate are continuous? Is it ok to round them post-hoc? Do those rounded values then truly correspond to the probabilities that generated them?

It looks like the RNGforGPD package will solve my problem (thank you again for that), but please let me know if it would help to give any further explanation on the mid-posterior p-values. And if you have any insights for me regarding the questions in the previous paragraph, please do let me know.

Thanks again for all you do.
Rebecca

messages.body_plain:
I've had a recent problem getting zero-inflated Poisson models to run using HMC samplers on several different ZIP models. I've tried a few modifications with no luck. The chains are stuck at initial values unless I change the parameters samplers to RW, then sampling works. Is this a software limitation or is there anything else I can try to get this working? I could really use the speed up in convergence.

Things I've tried:
(1) Using the ZIP distribution function provided on the nimble help docs here:
https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/zero_inflated_poisson.html
and the latent parameterization.
(2) Changing the HMC samplers to RW samplers for various parameters.

I realize this is not a reproducible example, but it's happened every time I've tried to use a ZIP model. I can provide code if needed for troubleshooting, but I wanted to check that it's not something obvious first.

Nimble has been an extremely useful tool for my work, so I appreciate all the work and developement going into this package.
Cheers,
Brian

messages.subject_clean: sampling N in N-mixture models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nimble team,

I'm trying to write my own Nimble sampler for N (the true abundance) in N-mixture models. This is some kind of Poisson random walk that is introduced in the Hooten & Hefley book and looks like the following if it's written in R:

### Sample N
N_star <- rpois(nsite, N + N_tune) # N_tune is normally set to 1
mh1 <- apply(dbinom(y, N_star, p, log=T), 1, sum) +
       dpois(N_star, lambda, log=T) +
       dpois(N, N_star+N_tune, log=T)
mh2 <- apply(dbinom(y, N     , p, log=T), 1, sum) +
       dpois(N     , lambda, log=T) +
       dpois(N_star, N+N_tune, log=T)
mh <- exp(mh1 - mh2)
Nkeep <- ((mh > runif(nsite)) & (N_star >= ymax))
N[Nkeep] <- N_star[Nkeep]

I wrote the following Nimble function, which (unsurprisingly) doesn't work:

Poisson_RW <- nimbleFunction(

    contains = sampler_BASE,

    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        # proposal standard deviation
        scale <- if(!is.null(control$scale)) control$scale else 1
        calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
    },

    run = function() {
        # initial model logProb
        model_lp_initial <- getLogProb(model, calcNodes)
        # generate proposal
        proposal <- rpois(1, model[[target]] + scale)
        # store proposal into model
        model[[target]] <<- proposal
        # proposal model logProb
        model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)

        # log-Metropolis-Hastings ratio
        log_MH_ratio <- model_lp_proposed - model_lp_initial

        # Metropolis-Hastings step: determine whether or
        # not to accept the newly proposed value
        u <- runif(1, 0, 1)
        if(u < exp(log_MH_ratio)) jump <- TRUE
        else                      jump <- FALSE

        # keep the model and mvSaved objects consistent
        if(jump) copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1,
                         nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
        else     copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1,
                         nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
    },

    methods = list(   reset = function () {}   )
)

I have several questions:

1. When I try to compile the model, I encountered the following error message:

> compiled <- compileNimble(model, mcmc)
Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Failed to create the shared library. Run 'printErrors()' to see the compilation errors.

When I run 'printErrors()', I got more error messages, the first a few lines of which look like this:

P_3_MCMC.cpp: In member function 'void sampler_RW_block::adaptiveProcedure(bool)':
P_3_MCMC.cpp:321:5: warning: variable 'Interm_69' set but not used [-Wunused-but-set-variable]
  321 | int Interm_69;
      |     ^~~~~~~~~

Since these error messages are beyond my scope of understanding, I wonder what exactly went wrong. I understand that the sampler must be incomplete, but I don't understand why it doesn't run at all.

2. Concerning the incompleteness of the sampler, I would assume that the line "model_lp_initial <- getLogProb(model, calcNodes)" naturally realizes the first two parts of mh2, i.e., "apply(dbinom(y, N, p, log=T), 1, sum) + dpois(N, lambda, log=T)", but I wonder how to include the last part, "dpois(N_star, N+N_tune, log=T)", in the Nimble code. Please let me know if my understanding is entirely wrong.

3. Again, I may be entirely wrong, but my understanding is that, in the R code, we have two criteria when deciding to keep or update N. In addition to having "mh" as the probability of acceptance, we also constrain N to be greater than or equal to ymax. This second criterion is naturally realized in the Nimble code because "model_lp_proposed" would be -Inf if N is smaller than ymax, which leads to "exp(log_MH_ratio)" being 0. Please let me know if I got it wrong.

Any help will be greatly appreciated. A script including everything is attached.

Best regards,
Qing

messages.subject: Re: HMC samplers stuck with ZIP
messages.subject_clean: HMC samplers stuck with ZIP
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian,
Below are two versions of the example. The first uses the marginalized dZIP and makes it work with AD. Conditionals such as "if(x != 0)" do not work with AD, so it had to be re-written to represent a continuous function of parameters without any if-then-else statements. The type of x also needed to be changed to double(). The second version uses a latent variable for z[i] and works as intended. In both cases one needs to turn on AD via the buildDerivs argument(s). I couldn't exactly follow which case you wanted, but I hope these cover the options and get you started. I realized the example of the web page uses p as probability of a structural zero, whereas often in model code it is flipped to probability of a one (such as presence, or alive, etc). I flipped it in the first example to match what I thought was the natural way to write the second example.
Perry

library(nimble)
library(nimbleHMC)

######
## First version: modify r-nimble example to support AD and HMC
#####

ZIPcode <- nimbleCode({
  p ~ dunif(0,1) # this was probability of absence, but I flipped it...
  lambda ~ dunif(0,10)
  for (i in 1:N)
    y[i] ~ dZIP(lambda, zeroProb = 1-p) # ... to be probability of presence
})

dZIP <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(x = double(), lambda = double(),
                zeroProb = double(), log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
   returnType(double())
   ## First handle non-zero data
   prob <- zeroProb * dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = 0) + (1 - zeroProb) * dpois(x, lambda)
   if (log) return(log(prob))
   return(prob)
 },
 buildDerivs = 'run'
 )

rZIP <- nimbleFunction(
 run = function(n = integer(), lambda = double(), zeroProb = double()) {
   returnType(double())
   isStructuralZero <- rbinom(1, prob = zeroProb, size = 1)
   if (isStructuralZero) return(0)
   return(rpois(1, lambda))
})

registerDistributions(list(
    dZIP = list(
        BUGSdist = "dZIP(lambda, zeroProb)",
        discrete = TRUE,
        range = c(0, Inf),
        types = c('value = double()', 'lambda = double()', 'zeroProb = double()')
     )))

ZIPmodel <- nimbleModel(ZIPcode, constants = list(N = 100),
                        buildDerivs=TRUE)
ZIPmodel$p <- .6             ## Choose values of p and lambda
ZIPmodel$lambda <- 1.8
set.seed(1)
ZIPmodel$simulate(ZIPmodel$getDependencies(c("p", "lambda"), self=FALSE))       ## Simulate values of y[1]...y[100]
simulatedData <- ZIPmodel$y
simulatedData
ZIPmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedData))  ## Set those values as data in the model
cZIPmodel <- compileNimble(ZIPmodel)

ZIPmcmc <- buildHMC(ZIPmodel)
cZIPmcmc <- compileNimble(ZIPmcmc, project = ZIPmodel)

samples <- runMCMC(cZIPmcmc)
# Per message, the second half are the valid HMC samples
# although in this case they all look similar
summary(samples[5001:10000,])

######
## Second version: use discrete latent state and combination of samplers
#####

ZIPcode2 <- nimbleCode({
  p ~ dunif(0,1)
  lambda ~ dunif(0,10)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    z[i] ~ dbern(p)
    y[i] ~ dpois(lambda*z[i]) ## Note NIMBLE allows R-like named-parameter syntax
  }
})

zData <- rep(1, 100)
boolZero <- simulatedData == 0
zData[ boolZero ] <- NA
zInits <- rep(NA, 100)
zInits[ boolZero ] <- rbinom(sum(boolZero), size = 1, prob = 0.5)

ZIPmodel2 <- nimbleModel(ZIPcode2, constants = list(N = 100),
                         data = list(y = simulatedData, z = zData),
                         inits = list(z = zInits),
                        buildDerivs=TRUE)
cZIPmodel2 <- compileNimble(ZIPmodel2)

ZIPmcmc2 <- buildHMC(ZIPmodel2, monitors = c("lambda", "p", "z"))
cZIPmcmc2 <- compileNimble(ZIPmcmc2, project = ZIPmodel2)

samples2 <- runMCMC(cZIPmcmc2)

Hi all,

I am learning how to implement Dirichlet process mixture models in nimble using both the Chinese Restaurant Process and the stick-breaking representation.

I noticed at the bottom of the tutorial here <https://r-nimble.org/bayesian-nonparametric-models-in-nimble-part-1-density-estimation>, there is mention of future development in nimble of new advances in Bayesian non-parametrics, including hierarchical Dirichlet processes (HDPs).

I was wondering if there is any new development with respect to HDPs being implemented in nimble. If not, is there a way to program a HDP in the current version of nimble?

Thanks in advance!
Jake

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the additional information.

I admit upfront I have not completely processed and understood your model.  That said, following are some statements, which, with varying degrees of confidence, I believe are true.  If any of these are false, please let me know.

- You are providing observed numbers for "x_multi_j", and these numbers are being passed into the model as "data".
- None of the numbers being provided for "x_multi_j" are NA.
- Therefore, no samplers are being assigned to any elements of "x_multi_j".  That is, "x_multi_j" does not appear anywhere in the Samplers section of the printed MCMC configuration object.
- You are providing values for "tot_j" through either the "constants" list, or the "data" list, when constructing the model.

- When using the U(0, 1) prior distribution for truePM_st[s,t], some values in the interval (0,1) can produce negative values of rho_stb[...]
- When using the more constrained prior distribution:

       dunif(omega_st[s,t] * (1- rho_env_st[s,t] ), rho_env_st[s,t]  + (omega_st[s,t] * (1-rho_env_st[s,t] )))

for truePM_st[s,t], the values of rho_stb[...] cannot go negative.

- In the uncertainty plots you sent, the plots shown for quantities such as rhoFN, rhoTP, rhoUN, etc, represent values from the model of rho_stb[s,t,index], for different values of "index".

- Your original concern has been resolved and addressed.

Thanks!
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: sampling N in N-mixture models
messages.subject_clean: sampling N in N-mixture models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Qing,

Thanks for posting the question.

By the way, the printErrors() output you copied is actually just a warning and is not a problem. But there is an actual error as well.

The problem is that you have assigned the samplet to the entire vector 'N'. If you want it to expand "N" into scalar nodes and assign the sampler to each one (which I think is what you want), please add "expandTarget=TRUE". When I do that, your code runs on my system (although the resulting MCMC does not mix well).  If you want to make this a block sampler (more like what the R code does, taking vectorized steps for all of N), then leave expandTarget=FALSE but avoid "model[[target]]", which assumes target is one node, and instead use values(model, target). However it would be more complicated to separate the calcNodes into groups of nodes corresponding to each N, so I don't recommend this and there wouldn't be much if any benefit to it. Also please remember you can run uncompiled and use R debugging to check on the logic (although this doesn't always catch issues that will cause C++ compiler errors, because the R interpreter does some run-time flexible behaviors that don't work for the nimble compiler.)

I think there are a few things going on in your further questions. First, we recommend the more modern nimble syntax "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)". That gets the sum of the log probabilities of the calcNodes that are stored from the current state of the model, without recalculation. I agree with your interpretation in relation to mh2 (although the mh1 and mh2 code is vectorized over all N, whereas you will want to do one N at a time, I presume, as just discussed).

The last parts of mh1 and mh2 look like the numerator and denominator of the log proposal probability ratio. In many samplers, these cancel, but in your case they will not. You can simply calculate them manually using e.g "dpois(model[[target]], proposal + scale, log=TRUE) - dpois(proposal, model[[target]] + scale, log=TRUE)" (and add that to your log_MH_ratio). Please check that I got that right. Obviously you'll want to do that before "model[[target]] <- proposal". We often find it convenient to do "current <- model[[target]]" (and then use "current" instead of "model[[target]]" repeatedly) first to make the code easier to follow and slightly less error-prone (and potentially a microsecond faster).

Regarding the lower bound at ymax, I'd suggest three options. The first is, as you say, to simply let the proposals be rejected because logProb=-Inf. That should be valid. The second is to split up the calcNodes into one piece with the target and another piece with the dependencies (with "self=FALSE"). Then you can first do just "model$calculate(target)" (i.e. calculate the prior for the proposal) and reject if that is -Inf without wasting computation on all the other dependencies. If model$calculate(target) is not -Inf, then you can proceed with the rest of the MH calculations and steps. Many of our samplers take this approach. A final option is to reflect the sampler off of ymax, e.g. for proposal < ymax, set proposal = ymax + (ymax-proposal). If you do that, you must always include the possible reflection in the log proposal probabilities, so only do that if what I just said makes sense.

HTH.
Perry

messages.body_plain:
The model object stores (aka caches) the most recently calculated value of the log probability of any stochastic node. model$getLogProb simply accesses these stored values, which is much faster than calculating them again. The protocol for nimble's MCMC scheme is that every sampler can expect to start with all calculations up-to-date (including values of deterministic nodes and log probabilities of stochastic nodes) and is required to finish with all calculations up-to-date. So when obtaining the relevant log probabilities for the "current" state of the model, before changing any values in the model, it is safe for a sampler to use model$getLogProb. After proposing a new value (i.e. changing the value of a stochastic node in the model), calculations need to be updated, so one must use model$calculate. HTH. You can play with a model object (assign values and use getLogProb and calculate in different orders) to make sense of it.
Cheers,
Perry

> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Packages submitted to CRAN should not have any compiled code in them (i.e., they are "source" packages containing only source code). This is, in part, because the compiled code will differ by operating system.

If you build the package with `R CMD build` is the package size still so large? I wouldn't think it would be -- `compileNimble` shouldn't be being invoked.
More generally, you should only have `compileNimble` being invoked inside of functions in your packages -- so it would only be called when a user of your package runs one of your functions. Nothing in your code should cause `compileNimble` to be called when `R CMD build` or `R CMD INSTALL --build` are run. (The latter creates binary packages from the source package, which is what CRAN does to create the MacOS and Windows binaries after you submit your package to CRAN.)

I'm happy to discuss further as you investigate more.

-chris

Dear Perry,

Thank you very much for your response. It really worked after I made changes accordingly!!

This Poisson random walk sampler cut the running time from 45 seconds (for slice sampler) to 35 seconds, for 5000 iterations. However, I haven't compared the efficiency of the two samplers, so I'm still not sure which one is better. In any case, I attached the code in case anyone is interested.

Just out of curiosity, I believe we calculate the lop probability of the current value by using "model_lp_initial <- model$getLogProb(calcNodes)", and log probability of the proposed value by using "model_lp_proposed <- model$calculate(calcNodes)". What is the reason we use "getLogProb" for one but "calculate" for the other?

Thanks again for the help. It's greatly appreciated.

Best,

> Dear Qing,
>
> Thanks for posting the question.
>
> By the way, the printErrors() output you copied is actually just a warning and is not a problem. But there is an actual error as well.
>
> The problem is that you have assigned the samplet to the entire vector 'N'. If you want it to expand "N" into scalar nodes and assign the sampler to each one (which I think is what you want), please add "expandTarget=TRUE". When I do that, your code runs on my system (although the resulting MCMC does not mix well).  If you want to make this a block sampler (more like what the R code does, taking vectorized steps for all of N), then leave expandTarget=FALSE but avoid "model[[target]]", which assumes target is one node, and instead use values(model, target). However it would be more complicated to separate the calcNodes into groups of nodes corresponding to each N, so I don't recommend this and there wouldn't be much if any benefit to it. Also please remember you can run uncompiled and use R debugging to check on the logic (although this doesn't always catch issues that will cause C++ compiler errors, because the R interpreter does some run-time flexible behaviors that don't work for the nimble compiler.)
>
> I think there are a few things going on in your further questions. First, we recommend the more modern nimble syntax "model$getLogProb(calcNodes)". That gets the sum of the log probabilities of the calcNodes that are stored from the current state of the model, without recalculation. I agree with your interpretation in relation to mh2 (although the mh1 and mh2 code is vectorized over all N, whereas you will want to do one N at a time, I presume, as just discussed).
>
> The last parts of mh1 and mh2 look like the numerator and denominator of the log proposal probability ratio. In many samplers, these cancel, but in your case they will not. You can simply calculate them manually using e.g "dpois(model[[target]], proposal + scale, log=TRUE) - dpois(proposal, model[[target]] + scale, log=TRUE)" (and add that to your log_MH_ratio). Please check that I got that right. Obviously you'll want to do that before "model[[target]] <- proposal". We often find it convenient to do "current <- model[[target]]" (and then use "current" instead of "model[[target]]" repeatedly) first to make the code easier to follow and slightly less error-prone (and potentially a microsecond faster).
>
> Regarding the lower bound at ymax, I'd suggest three options. The first is, as you say, to simply let the proposals be rejected because logProb=-Inf. That should be valid. The second is to split up the calcNodes into one piece with the target and another piece with the dependencies (with "self=FALSE"). Then you can first do just "model$calculate(target)" (i.e. calculate the prior for the proposal) and reject if that is -Inf without wasting computation on all the other dependencies. If model$calculate(target) is not -Inf, then you can proceed with the rest of the MH calculations and steps. Many of our samplers take this approach. A final option is to reflect the sampler off of ymax, e.g. for proposal < ymax, set proposal = ymax + (ymax-proposal). If you do that, you must always include the possible reflection in the log proposal probabilities, so only do that if what I just said makes sense.
>
> HTH.
> Perry

> The model object stores (aka caches) the most recently calculated value of the log probability of any stochastic node. model$getLogProb simply accesses these stored values, which is much faster than calculating them again. The protocol for nimble's MCMC scheme is that every sampler can expect to start with all calculations up-to-date (including values of deterministic nodes and log probabilities of stochastic nodes) and is required to finish with all calculations up-to-date. So when obtaining the relevant log probabilities for the "current" state of the model, before changing any values in the model, it is safe for a sampler to use model$getLogProb. After proposing a new value (i.e. changing the value of a stochastic node in the model), calculations need to be updated, so one must use model$calculate. HTH. You can play with a model object (assign values and use getLogProb and calculate in different orders) to make sense of it.
> Cheers,
> Perry

messages.subject: Re: hierarchical Dirichlet processes
messages.subject_clean: hierarchical Dirichlet processes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob,

We had some work planned to implement the HDP, but that never reached fruition. It should be possible to program in nimble, perhaps building on ideas
from our existing CRP sampler (see the file "BNP_samplers.R"). I'll note that much of the complication in the existing CRP sampler is in the setup code
for the sampler, which does a lot of checking to make sure the sampler is valid for the model structure given by a user. If you were coding it for your own
use you could presumably skip that complication.

I'm checking with some colleagues who did much of the work on the CRP sampler to see if they have any useful information to share on HDP.

-chris
